The Blue lanternfish (Tarletonbeania crenularis) is a mesopelagic myctophid common in the North Pacific, where individuals undergo a pronounced allometric shift during the larval-juvenile transition. Morphometric analysis of field-collected specimens indicates that the standard length at which metamorphosis initiates is approximately 1.7 cm , with a subsequent developmental gap extending to about 2.17 cm during which the body plan reorganisation of the metamorphic climax is completed. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from transparent, pelagic eggs at an extremely modest size; based on an egg diameter comparable to that of the related Diaphus dumerilii, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.000065 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000065 grams]. This lecithotrophic prolarva depends entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth opens and first feeding commences, a trophic switch that must occur before the point of no return is reached.

At the ambient temperatures typical of the species' mesopelagic habitat, sustained at approximately 6.2 °C [T = 6.2 °C], the maximum reproductive output of female Tarletonbeania crenularis becomes a key demographic parameter. Under these thermal conditions, the estimated maximum fecundity per reproductive event combined with spawning frequency yields a daily egg production rate that is consistent with a kap-type life-history strategy. Specifically, field surveys and comparative ovary analyses indicate that females produce roughly 40000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 40000 eggs per spawning event], and with approximately one spawning event each year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event each year], the potential annual reproductive effort is substantial for a fish of this size. This reproductive schedule is maintained within the stable thermal regime of 6.2 °C [T = 6.2 °C] that characterises the depths they inhabit.

Sexual maturation in Tarletonbeania crenularis occurs at a body size that is intermediate relative to the maximum length the species can attain. The standard length at puberty, defined by the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation onset, is recorded at 4.9 cm [Lp = 4.9 cm], a value derived by comparing the relative length at maturity of the related Diaphus dumerilii. Concomitantly, the wet weight at puberty for females is estimated at 1.4 grams [Wwp = 1.4 grams], which represents a considerable increase from the initial larval mass. Puberty is reached after a period of steady growth during the exogenously feeding pelagic larval phase and subsequent post-metamorphic juvenile stage. The attainment of this size threshold appears to be a reliable predictor of reproductive activation, as gravid individuals are only encountered above this length.

The ultimate body size of female Blue lanternfish is a critical determinant of their lifetime reproductive potential. Analysis of length-frequency distributions from midwater trawls indicates that the maximum recorded adult standard length approaches 12.7 cm [Li = 12.7 cm], while the corresponding asymptotic body mass derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship reaches approximately 27 grams [Wwi = approximately 27 grams] for the largest females. This ultimate wet weight represents a near five-hundredfold increase from the wet weight at puberty and a more than four-hundred-thousandfold increase from the neonatal mass, reflecting the substantial somatic investment undertaken before reproduction begins. The length-weight allometry itself, calculated as 0.01023 times length in centimetres raised to the 3.10 power, is similar to that reported for other mesopelagic lanternfishes.

Longevity in Tarletonbeania crenularis is constrained by the cold, low-energy environment it occupies, with the maximum lifespan in the wild estimated at 2 years [am = 2 years] under the prevailing habitat temperature of 6.2 °C [T = 6.2 °C]. This relatively brief lifespan is typical of smaller myctophids and contrasts with the longer-lived species that occupy higher-latitude or deeper-dwelling niches within the family. The rapid life cycle, from early puberty at 4.9 cm [Lp = 4.9 cm] standard length to the maximal adult weight of 27 grams [Wwi = 27 grams], typifies a strategy that prioritizes high turnover over extended somatic growth. Such a strategy is well-suited to a species that forms a critical trophic link between zooplankton and higher predators in the productive North Pacific Current system.
